title: A Great Experience Begins at the Front Door : Reflections from VenueConnect 2026
summary: Hear from Lori Garza, senior manager of customer enablement, on her key takeaways after returning for the 10th year to IAVM's VenueConnect.
body_markdown:
Coming from the performing arts world, I’ve always believed the guest experience begins long before the show starts. Before the curtain rises, orchestra begins, or the first line of dialogue is delivered, guests are already forming opinions about their experience.


They’re evaluating parking, wayfinding, ticketing, staff interactions, wait times, and perhaps most importantly, their arrival at the venue. This ultimately defines the entire experience. That perspective was reinforced repeatedly during our conversations at IAVM VenueConnect last week.


## Guest Service Is an Entrance Strategy


As I sit here looking at the 10-year IAVM anniversary pin I received at VenueConnect this year, I find myself reflecting on how much our industry has evolved over the past decade. One theme stood out repeatedly throughout the conference: guest experience and venue operations can no longer be viewed as separate priorities. One reason is that the guest journey itself has changed dramatically.


Today, that connection is more important than ever. A patron can purchase tickets, receive event updates, access mobile tickets, and even get questions answered without ever speaking to another person. By the time they arrive at the venue, their first in-person interaction may be with a security officer, usher, or guest services team member at the front door.


That’s a responsibility we shouldn’t underestimate. Those first moments set the tone for the entire experience. When guests are welcomed with efficiency, professionalism, and dignity, that interaction becomes the beginning of a positive experience rather than an obstacle standing in the way of it.


Every decision made at the front door contributes to how guests feel about what follows.


For many people, attending a performance is more than simply going to a show.


They’ve:


- Blocked their calendar


- Arranged dinner reservations


- Coordinated schedules


- Secured childcare


- Purchased tickets often months in advance.


By the time they arrive, they expect to enjoy themselves, not worry about getting through the front door.


## The First Impression Is Often the Longest Lasting


During my years at the Denver Performing Arts Complex, I learned firsthand how much an arrival experience influences patron perception.


Guests rarely talk about the security experience when it works well.


But they almost always remember it when it doesn’t.


A smooth arrival experience benefits more than guests. It enables frontline staff to do what they do best: welcome, assist, and connect with patrons. When the arrival experience creates unnecessary friction, those same employees can find themselves managing frustration instead of delivering hospitality.


Long lines, confusion, bottlenecks, and inconsistent communication can quickly become part of the story people tell about their evening.


#### A smooth arrival, on the other hand, allows for:


- More time to enjoy the venue


- Visit concessions


- Interact with staff


- Settle in with a positive mindset


Throughout my career, I’ve often said that the best security programs support the guest experience rather than interrupt it. When arrival creates friction, what should be a simple conversation between a guest and a staff member, can quickly become a confrontation. But when safety, operations, and hospitality work together, guests don’t just feel secure, they feel welcomed. And that feeling often sets the tone for everything that follows.


## Safety and Hospitality Should Work Together


Another notable takeaway from VenueConnect was how venue leaders are increasingly discussing safety as part of hospitality. That is especially relevant in performing arts venues.


Guests should never have to choose between feeling welcome and feeling safe. The very best venue experiences deliver both.


The most successful venue environments create a sense of confidence without creating anxiety or unnecessary friction. They balance strong operational practices with a dignified, warm, welcoming atmosphere that patrons expect.


## Creating Experiences Worth Returning For


Throughout the conference, there was significant discussion around experience as a competitive advantage.


For performing arts organizations, that idea resonates deeply.


Guests may attend a specific performance because they love the artist, orchestra, ballet, or production. But the overall venue experience often influences whether they choose to return.


A great show matters.


A great experience matters just as much.


That includes:


- How guests are greeted


- How easily they enter


- How they move through the facility


- How they feel throughout their visit.


As many performing arts organizations continue to navigate changing audience expectations, focusing on these foundational elements remains one of the most effective ways to strengthen loyalty and create lasting relationships.


## Looking Forward


VenueConnect 2026 highlighted many important industry discussions, from leadership and collaboration to technology and innovation.


But the theme I kept returning to was simple: People remember how a venue makes them feel.


The entrance experience sets the tone for everything that follows. When guest services, operations, and safety work together, venues create more than an efficient arrival experience. They create a foundation for trust, comfort, and connection.


In a world where the first human interaction a guest has may be at the front door, that responsibility matters more than ever. The goal isn’t simply to move people through security. It’s to create a welcoming arrival experience and ensure that what should be a conversation never becomes an unnecessary confrontation.


And in performing arts venues especially, that’s exactly how every great performance should begin.
